title: Whither thou goest (Ruth 1)
hook: a Moabite widow refuses to leave her mother-in-law: thy people shall be my people

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samson, the strongest man in the book, undone by his own choices and saved at the end by a prayer. Your line was strength isn't wisdom. When did you pause before acting? Day three hundred ninety-five.

Three widows stand on a road. One is old: Naomi, Noemi in the Douay-Rheims. She left Bethlehem in a famine with her husband and two sons, and in the land of Moab she buried all three. The other two are young, Moabite women who married her sons. Now Naomi is walking home with nothing, and she stops and tells them: go back. Go home to your mothers. I have no more sons for you. There's nothing for you where I'm going. They cry. One of them, Orpah, kisses her and turns back, and nobody in the story blames her. The other one won't let go. Her name is Ruth.
screen: `THREE WIDOWS ON A ROAD.` → `GO HOME TO YOUR MOTHERS.` → `ONE TURNS BACK. ONE WON'T.`

segments.voice: What Ruth says next, many people know by heart without knowing where it comes from. Most English speakers know it from the King James: "whither thou goest, I will go." The Douay-Rheims gives it like this: "whithersoever thou shalt go, I will go: and where thou shalt dwell, I also will dwell. Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." And she goes further: where you die, I'll die, and there I'll be buried. Notice who she's saying it to. Not a husband. A mother-in-law, old, grieving and broke, who has just told her to leave. Couples often read these words at weddings, and that's lovely. But first they were a daughter-in-law's vow to a widow with nothing to offer. The Hebrew storytellers have a word for what Ruth does: chesed, steady, loyal love that keeps showing up. Naomi even uses it on the road, praying that God will deal kindly with the two young women, as they have dealt with the dead and with her. Ruth is a foreigner, from Moab, a people Israel had old quarrels with. And she becomes, in this book, the picture of faithfulness. Then they reach Bethlehem, and the town women say, is this Naomi? And Naomi answers, in the Douay: "I went out full, and the Lord hath brought me back empty." Don't call me Naomi, she says, which means beautiful. Call me Mara, bitter. The book lets her say it. It doesn't correct her or rush her. It just keeps Ruth standing beside her, through the bitterness, at the start of the barley harvest.
screen: `WHITHER THOU GOEST, I WILL GO.` · `A VOW TO A MOTHER-IN-LAW.` · `CHESED — LOVE THAT STAYS.` · `CALL ME MARA, BITTER.` · then, large: `THY PEOPLE SHALL BE MY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay with someone going through loss. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who is grieving right now. A death, a divorce, a job, a diagnosis, a move they didn't want. Maybe, like Naomi, they've told everyone they're fine, or told everyone to go away. Picture yourself on the road beside them, not fixing anything, just walking. Ask what staying would look like this week. A message that doesn't need an answer. A meal. Sitting through the bitter part. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name. The bell holds the time.
Whither thou goest. Ruth's promise to Naomi, a vow of loyal love from a foreign daughter-in-law to a widow who had nothing left. Today's word.
Your line: thy people, my people. Today, reach out to one grieving person and stay a little longer than is comfortable. Day three hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Ruth's story in the weekday Mass readings, and her promise to Naomi is one of the Old Testament readings couples may choose for a Catholic wedding.

she said them to Naomi, her widowed mother-in-law, on the road to Bethlehem.

a foreigner, and the book makes her the picture of loyal love.

Naomi told both to go back. Orpah obeys, kisses her and leaves, and the text doesn't condemn her.

fork.setup: you're Ruth. your husband is dead, your mother-in-law is going back to a country you've never seen, and she's told you to go home. what do you do?
options: kiss her goodbye and go home, like Orpah.
promise to go where she goes, live where she lives, and be buried where she's buried.
go with her as far as the border.
fork.reveal: Ruth won't leave: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God. a vow of loyal love made to a widow with nothing to give back.

original.note: Hebrew: loyal, steadfast love. Naomi uses it on the road, and it runs through the whole Book of Ruth.

trapdoor: what you thought: a romantic vow, read at weddings.
what it means: a young foreign widow refuses to leave her grieving mother-in-law, and binds her life, her people and her God to Naomi's.
what a scholar hears: chesed, loyal love, is a key word of the book. Naomi asks God to show it in 1:8, and Ruth lives it out on the road.

notes: The title phrase is the KJV's; the Douay has 'whithersoever thou shalt go'. Both are quoted and cited.
Ruth 1:16–17 as an optional Old Testament reading for Catholic weddings: confirm it is in the current Order of Celebrating Matrimony lectionary list; soften if not.
Chesed in Ruth 1:8 (Douay: 'deal mercifully'): confirm the Hebrew word and the paraphrase 'deal kindly'.
Naomi = 'pleasant/beautiful', Mara = 'bitter' follows the Douay's own glosses in 1:20.
